section_summary: This section concerns Japan’s ability to finance the war in China and the possibility of foreign loans or credits. It includes diplomatic reporting on gold shipments and bond purchases, a detailed assessment of Japan’s financial reserves, and correspondence opposing a reported $50 million credit for heavy industry in Manchukuo. The final memorandum reports a claim that Japan had delayed payment to Germany for industrial machinery.

subfiles.title: File note on Grew’s telegram about foreign capital
subfiles.about: Points to Grew’s report on British proposals concerning loans to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references telegram 596 and its discussion of Craigie’s proposed cable.

subfiles.title: Grew on proposed British approach to loans for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Craigie’s proposal to coordinate responses to Japanese requests for financial assistance.
subfiles.summary: Craigie argued that credits could prolong hostilities and proposed making assistance depend on peace terms. Grew warned that this might imply an American commitment to lend and doubted that American financiers would provide capital.

subfiles.title: File note on French support for withholding finance
subfiles.about: Points to Grew’s telegram on the French colleague’s position.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references telegram 601 on French support for Craigie’s suggestions.

subfiles.title: Grew on French support for Craigie’s proposal
subfiles.about: Reports that the French ambassador supported Craigie’s proposed approach to Japanese financing.
subfiles.summary: The French colleague had cabled his government in general agreement with Craigie.

subfiles.title: Japanese gold shipments to the United States
subfiles.about: Reports two Bank of Japan gold shipments and its plan to stop shipments for the year.
subfiles.summary: The Bank shipped 208,000 ounces on November 30 and 331,000 ounces on December 11.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of telegram 627 on Japanese gold shipments
subfiles.about: Restates Grew’s report of Japanese gold shipments.
subfiles.summary: Lists the November 30 and December 11 shipments and says no more were planned in 1937.

subfiles.title: Transmission of gold-shipment telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of the paraphrase of Grew’s telegram 627.
subfiles.summary: Encloses six copies of the gold-shipment paraphrase.

subfiles.title: Feis on Treasury meeting with Japanese Financial Attaché
subfiles.about: Asks whether to attend a Treasury meeting likely to concern Japanese gold shipments.
subfiles.summary: A handwritten instruction records a decision that Feis should not attend.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese government finance
subfiles.about: Points to Grew’s despatch on optimistic statements by Japanese financial leaders.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch 2654 on Japan’s financial condition.

subfiles.title: Extract on government finance and foreign trade
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese official claims and trade controls during October 1937.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials expressed confidence in war financing and approved budget savings. The extract reports an October trade surplus and restrictions on imports, exports, and cotton supplies.

subfiles.title: File note on U.S. policy toward foreign loans
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram addressing Craigie’s question about American loan policy.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references telegram 338 on foreign loans and the Far Eastern situation.

subfiles.title: File note on the Japanese budget
subfiles.about: Points to Grew’s despatch on government finance and the 1938–39 budget.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch 2686, including the draft budget excluding further military expenditure.

subfiles.title: Extract on Japan’s draft 1938–39 budget
subfiles.about: Reports financial optimism, possible tax increases, and Cabinet approval of a draft budget.
subfiles.summary: The draft budget omitted estimates for continuing military operations in China.

subfiles.title: Bullitt asks about Ford’s Japanese bond purchase
subfiles.about: Seeks confirmation that Ford’s Japanese subsidiary subscribed to China Incident bonds.
subfiles.summary: A Havas report said the subsidiary bought one million yen in bonds; Bullitt asked whether it was true.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to Tokyo about Ford bond purchase
subfiles.about: Requests confirmation of Ford’s reported bond purchase and comment on exchange restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks Tokyo to investigate a reported one-million-yen purchase.

subfiles.title: Grew confirms Ford bond purchase
subfiles.about: Explains the connection between Ford’s bond purchase and permission to remit dividends.
subfiles.summary: Ford bought one million yen in China Incident bonds after officials linked the purchase to permission to remit dividends. A similar proposal was made to Singer, which bought no bonds.

subfiles.title: Reply to Paris on Ford bond purchase
subfiles.about: Relays Grew’s findings on Ford’s bond purchase and remittance negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Quotes Tokyo’s confirmation and its comparison with Singer.

subfiles.title: Feis sends financial analysis to Burnett
subfiles.about: Sends a departmental-use analysis of Japan’s economic position.
subfiles.summary: Encloses “Observations on Japan’s Financial Position.”

subfiles.title: Feis’s covering memorandum on Japanese economic position
subfiles.about: Summarizes the conclusions of an analysis of Japan’s economic capacity.
subfiles.summary: Japan could sustain its present war with China for a long period, but a larger conflict would rapidly exhaust its resources.

subfiles.title: Observations on Japan’s Financial Position
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s internal borrowing capacity, foreign exchange reserves, and balance of payments.
subfiles.summary: The analysis disputes a newspaper account suggesting imminent financial crisis. It argues that Japanese banks and institutions can absorb further government bonds, while foreign exchange reserves could sustain current operations for months. Gold, overseas balances, and securities provide resources, though continued war would deplete them. Reconstruction in China would later create a need for foreign capital and could influence settlement terms.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Jay asks about Japanese bonds
subfiles.about: Requests advice about Japanese Oriental Development bonds held by her family.
subfiles.summary: Jay fears that repudiation of the bonds would wipe out savings from a former retail business.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. Jay about investment advice
subfiles.from: Herbert Feis, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Declines to advise whether she should sell Japanese Oriental Development bonds.
subfiles.summary: Feis says officials cannot recommend buying or selling securities and suggests market quotations and Commerce Department information.

subfiles.title: Thompson opposes proposed Manchukuo credit
subfiles.about: Urges opposition to a reported $50 million American credit for heavy industry in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Thompson argues that the credit could support Japan’s war in China and encloses a missionary’s account of conditions there.

subfiles.title: Missionary letter on the war in China
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese bombing, civilian suffering, and fears about the war’s wider consequences.
subfiles.summary: The missionary reports bombing of Chinese cities and damage to educational and medical institutions. The letter warns that continued conquest could spread conflict and push China toward Soviet Russia. It also describes Chinese Christian responses and urges greater international attention.

subfiles.title: Reply to Thompson about reported credit
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges her letter and addresses the reported American credit to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says the Department knows of no current American banking or commercial loans or credits to Japan.

subfiles.title: File note on Treasury emergency-powers memorandum
subfiles.about: Points to a Treasury memorandum on presidential powers under the Trading with the Enemy Act.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Herman Oliphant’s memorandum concerning national-emergency powers.

subfiles.title: Feis forwards British policy account
subfiles.about: Forwards an account of British policy toward credits to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Recalls Craigie’s inquiry and discussion at Brussels, then points to the attached parliamentary account.

subfiles.title: British policy toward loans to Japan
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Reviews House of Commons exchanges on loans to Japan and earlier British policy toward Italy.
subfiles.summary: British ministers said no current Japanese loan application was before them and referred to the principles used for Italy. The memorandum quotes restrictions on foreign security issues, commercially judged export credits excluding munitions, and limits on private credits. It also notes an American Embassy observation about Italian dollar securities.

subfiles.title: Quigley asks about American financing of belligerents
subfiles.about: Asks whether American institutions have lent to or otherwise financed China or Japan.
subfiles.summary: Quigley seeks information on loans, credits, and other financial assistance.

subfiles.title: Hamilton replies to Quigley
subfiles.about: States the Department’s knowledge of American financing since the conflict began.
subfiles.summary: No such loans or credits were known, apart from short-term merchandise and gold transit credits.

subfiles.title: Deutsman letter concerning a reported Japanese loan
subfiles.about: Raises concerns that Japan may be seeking a loan in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The incoming letter is mostly illegible; its subject and date are identified in the reply.

subfiles.title: Reply to Deutsman about a reported Japanese loan
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to concern about a possible American loan to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says the Department knows of no current American banking or commercial loans to Japan.

subfiles.title: Johnson reports Chinese protest against Manchukuo credit
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese organizations’ appeal against a proposed $50 million American credit.
subfiles.summary: Representatives warned that machinery for Manchukuo heavy industry could serve Japan’s war effort.

subfiles.title: Watson denies interest in Japanese machinery credits
subfiles.about: Reports Thomas J. Watson’s rejection of involvement in proposed Japanese machinery credits.
subfiles.summary: Watson says neither IBM nor the International Chamber of Commerce would seek or arrange the credits.

subfiles.title: Department relays Watson’s denial to Hankow
subfiles.about: Provides Watson’s published denial in response to Johnson’s report.
subfiles.summary: Quotes Watson’s statement that neither IBM nor the International Chamber would participate in the credits.

subfiles.title: Copy of Johnson’s telegram on Chinese credit protest
subfiles.about: Repeats the report of Chinese opposition to proposed Manchukuo machinery credits.
subfiles.summary: A second copy of telegram 45 records the delegation and its request to discourage the credit.

subfiles.title: Copy of Department’s reply to Hankow
subfiles.about: Repeats Watson’s published denial of involvement in Japanese credits.
subfiles.summary: A second copy of telegram 30 quotes Watson’s refusal to arrange the proposed credits.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Paul Scheffer on Japanese payments to Germany
subfiles.about: Records Scheffer’s claim that Japan postponed payment for German industrial machinery.
subfiles.summary: Scheffer speculated that Japan delayed payment because Germany was selling arms and other goods to China.
